questions.text: Which shape roles does it need?
questions.description: The elements that get their own corner.
One fixed set for the product, or a set per brand.
The corner of buttons and inputs.
The place where corners are seen most.

properties.title: Corner
properties.description: The radius of a box's corners.

jobs.description: A corner helps say what a thing is: a control, a status or a container.
jobs.how: Each kind keeps one corner, so people learn it. Shape is a second cue: pair it with size, color or words.
jobs.source: Material Design, the shape README: shapes identify components.

jobs.description: A corner carries the brand's feel. Sharp for precise, soft for calm and a pill for playful is brand convention, not research.
jobs.how: People prefer curved outlines, and sharp angles can read as a threat; the brand picks a curve for its feel.
jobs.source: Bar and Neta 2006, Humans prefer curved visual objects, Psychological Science 17(8). The three labels are brand convention.

jobs.description: A corner decides whether touching shapes read as separate objects (rounded) or as cells of one grid (square). A corner does not group: a shared fill or border groups.
jobs.how: A rounded corner breaks the outline, so touching shapes read apart; square corners meet and tile into one grid.
jobs.source: Palmer and Rock 1994, uniform connectedness; Wagemans et al. 2012. Grouping is common region (Palmer 1992), a job of fill and border.

jobs.description: Square corners align in dense rows; a large corner needs room, because the padding must be at least the radius.
jobs.how: A small curve keeps long straight edges that line up; a large curve cuts into the content box.
jobs.source: Cloud Four, The math behind nesting rounded corners.

jobs.description: An inner corner is the outer corner minus the padding, never under zero, so the shapes read as one family.
jobs.how: The inner curve follows the outer curve at the padding's distance, so the two edges stay concentric.
jobs.source: Cloud Four, The math behind nesting rounded corners; Apple's concentric corners.

jobs.description: The focus ring's corner is the control's corner plus the ring's offset, so the ring runs parallel to the control.
jobs.how: The same nesting rule, applied outward: the outer curve is the inner curve plus the gap.
jobs.source: Cloud Four, The math behind nesting rounded corners, applied outward.

properties.title: Line width
properties.description: The weight of the default border and divider. Its contrast lives in the color tokens.
properties.works_by: the weight and contrast of a stroke

jobs.description: A divider tells the eye where one region ends and the next starts. It decorates, so it has no contrast floor; space can often do the job instead.
jobs.how: A stroke between two regions breaks the surface, and its weight sets how strong the break reads.
jobs.source: WCAG 2.2, 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: decoration is exempt.

jobs.description: A border around a region groups what it holds.
jobs.how: A closed stroke draws a shared region, and the eye takes what is inside as one group.

jobs.description: Where the edge is the only sign that a control exists, the line must be seen: 3:1 against the colors next to it.
jobs.how: A stroke around the control marks its edge; its color sets the contrast and its weight how easy the edge is to find.

properties.title: Focus ring
properties.description: The ring around the control that has keyboard focus, and the gap between them.
properties.works_by: a heavier stroke with a gap

jobs.description: The ring shows where the keyboard is, on any surface.
jobs.how: A stroke one step heavier than the default line stands out from every border. The gap shows the page color between ring and control, so with two colors one keeps 3:1 against any fill.
jobs.source: WCAG 2.2, 2.4.7 and 2.4.13; W3C technique C40, two-color focus indicator.

relations.says: A decision: the corner answer says how controls look, the brand's feel sets the tone, and the density answer says how much room a corner gets.
A decision: the roles and count answers give containers their own corner, and the brand's feel sets its size. Control, badge and surface make as many sizes as the count answer names.
Derived: the surface corner minus the panel's padding, never under zero, so an option's corner stays concentric with its menu's.
Derived: the control corner, or the box corner when the control corner is a pill, because a box that grows cannot stay a pill.
Derived: the control corner, unless the roles answer gives badges a corner of their own.

A decision: the layering answer says whether lines separate groups, and the contrast floor says how heavy a line must be to be seen. The edge rule: a line that is the only cue that you can click or type is a boundary and needs 3:1. Importance picks its strength, and the same importance gets the same line, so every boundary reads color.border.strong. A line that is not the only cue stays faint, and quiet says why for each.

quiet.why: Each tab's label is the cue that it can be clicked. The line under the list only separates the tabs from the panel.
A static item cannot be clicked. Its edge only groups the item's content.

relations.says: Derived: one step heavier than the default line, so the ring stands out from every border. Focus is a state with its own look (accessibility.roles).

Fixed: a 2px gap between the control and its ring in every scheme. The gap is for contrast, not style: it shows the page color between ring and control, so one of the two colors keeps 3:1 on any fill (W3C technique C40).
